---
title: "Everyone Was Right: Lexical Representations in Language Models Are Both Abstract and Holistic"
author:
  - name: "Zachary Nicholas Houghton"
    affiliations:
      - name: "Vail Systems, Inc."
      - name: "University of Oregon"
    email: znh@uoregon.edu
  - name: "Yu Zhou"
    affiliations:
      - name: "Vail Systems, Inc."
  - name: "Dan Pluth"
    affiliations:
      - name: "Vail Systems, Inc."
  - name: "Vijay K. Gurbani"
    affiliations:
      - name: "Vail Systems, Inc."
  - name: "Vsevolod Kapatsinski"
    affiliations:
      - name: "University of Oregon"
abstract: |
  Lexical representations are central to linguistic theory, yet to what extent they're memorized or abstract remains a core debate. In the present study, we investigate this question in LLMs by decomposing contextual word representations into three additive components: an item component, a class component, and an idiosyncratic word-class interaction. After validating our measurement on an artificial language, we evaluate six pretrained transformers across two linguistic categories: part of speech and grammatical role. We find that the idiosyncratic interaction term is consistently positive and grows substantially across layers. Crucially, while item and class axes remain nearly orthogonal, the interaction term systematically overlaps with both. Together, our results demonstrate that LLMs learn representations that are simultaneously both abstract and holistic.
  
bibliography: refs.bib
acl-mode: review
code-url: https://github.com/znhoughton/representation-separability
anon-code-url: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/representation-separability-D254/
number-sections: true
tbl-cap-location: bottom
format:
  acl-pdf:
    keep-tex: true
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
# Force kable to emit raw LaTeX rather than markdown pipe tables. Without it pandoc builds the
# longtable itself and puts \bottomrule in \endlastfoot, which longtable typesets after the body,
# so the rule lands below the caption whenever tbl-cap-location is bottom.
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) options(knitr.table.format = "latex")
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(kableExtra)
library(patchwork); library(scales)

DATA <- file.path("..", "data")
# Reads a result CSV, falling back to the gzipped copy. validate_measure is 252,000 rows and is
# tracked compressed, with the plain file gitignored, so a fresh clone has only the .gz; readr
# decompresses transparently. Handled here rather than at the call site so any file can be
# compressed later without the paper needing to know.
rd <- function(f) {
  p <- file.path(DATA, f)
  if (!file.exists(p) && file.exists(paste0(p, ".gz"))) p <- paste0(p, ".gz")
  suppressMessages(read_csv(p, show_col_types = FALSE))
}

# Fill in columns a CSV predates, as NA, so a file measured before a field existed still loads
# and the affected numbers read as missing rather than bringing the whole render down.
ensure <- function(df, ...) {
  for (nm in c(...)) if (!nm %in% names(df)) df[[nm]] <- NA_real_
  df
}

# Green and gold are the University of Oregon colours, as in the companion papers; grey,
# amber and blue are supporting tones, not part of that palette. Green = the linear reference, gold = the
# nonlinearity; amber and blue are held for the model families in Experiments 2-3.
UO <- c(green = "#154733", green2 = "#007030", gold = "#F0B323",
        amber = "#875E00", blue = "#005581", grey = "#6E6E6E")
ACT_COL <- c(identity = UO[["green2"]], relu = UO[["gold"]])
ACT_LAB <- c(identity = "linear", relu = "ReLU")

theme_paper <- function(base = 9) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.25, color = "grey88"),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = base),
          legend.position = "top", legend.margin = margin(0, 0, -4, 0),
          legend.key.height = unit(9, "pt"),
          axis.title = element_text(size = base))
}

# ---- Experiment 1: the artificial-language grid ----
# 7,560 runs, measured with unified_split -- the SAME function and arguments Experiment 2
# uses. The two independent estimates are two even-sized splits of the observations for each item in each class, so there is
# no alignment step and no projection. Capacity is a reported variable, never a filter.
toy <- rd("artificial_language_grid.csv") |>
  ensure("obs_size_interaction", "size_interaction_excludes_zero",
         "obs_size_class", "size_class_excludes_zero",
         "size_item_excludes_zero") |>
  mutate(act = factor(activation, c("identity", "relu"), c("linear", "ReLU")),
         # An orthogonality reading means nothing on its own, so each overlap is carried
         # alongside the upper tail of its own null: the largest value an arbitrary orientation
         # produces in 97.5% of draws, from rotating the target subspace 200 times.
         null_hi = leak_item_into_class_null_hi,
         null_lo = leak_item_into_class_null_lo,
         null_med = leak_item_into_class_null_med,
         null_int = leak_int_into_margins_null_hi,
         null_int_lo = leak_int_into_margins_null_lo,
          null_int_med = leak_int_into_margins_null_med,
          # `ez` is the test the results are quoted with: the re-split 95% interval
          # excludes zero.
          ez = size_interaction_excludes_zero)

# Where no interaction was planted the linear arm is the floor, and by algebra it should be
# one: with additive inputs a linear map gives population means of the form A(f)+B(c), whose
# interaction is zero however much the language contains. Where an interaction WAS planted it
# is not at zero, because a trained linear model still carries whatever its contexts bring to
# each word and class -- see the Results. Both readings are the measure's at this exact width, sample
# size and context level.

# Does the measured interaction track the planted one? Binned, because the achieved share is
# continuous (neither the softmax nor the normalization is linear in the weights).
toy_track <- toy |> filter(w_item > 0, w_class > 0) |>
  mutate(bin = cut(ach_int, c(-Inf, .005, .05, .15, .30, .55, Inf),
                   labels = c("none", ".005-.05", ".05-.15", ".15-.30", ".30-.55", ">.55"))) |>
  group_by(act, bin) |>
  summarize(n = n(), ach = median(ach_int), size_int = median(size_interaction),
            lo = quantile(size_interaction, .25), hi = quantile(size_interaction, .75),
            flagged_ez = mean(ez, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# ---- what the learner builds, by width --------------------------------------------------------
# A run contributes only if the measure found structure for the three shares to divide: at least
# one of the three components has a re-split interval excluding zero. Where none does, the shares
# divide noise, whichever component lands slightly positive takes the whole of it, and the value
# is arbitrary rather than small. Every run this removes is at the narrowest width, and how many
# there are is reported in the Results rather than passed over.
toy_relu <- toy |> filter(act == "ReLU", w_item > 0, w_class > 0) |>
  mutate(resolved = size_item_excludes_zero | size_class_excludes_zero |
                   size_interaction_excludes_zero)
toy_unbuilt <- toy_relu |> group_by(d) |>
  summarize(runs = n(), none = sum(!resolved), pct = none / n(), .groups = "drop")

# Long form, one row per component, so the three can be drawn on one pair of axes. Intervals are
# the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles ACROSS RUNS: what the bar shows is how differently two runs of
# the same language at the same width come out, which is itself one of the findings.
toy_long <- toy_relu |> filter(resolved) |>
  select(d, ach_int, item = size_item, class = size_class, interaction = size_interaction) |>
  pivot_longer(c(item, class, interaction), names_to = "component", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, c("item", "class", "interaction")))

# One question asked three times: when the language holds a given amount of a component, how much
# of it does the learner build? Each component is matched against its OWN planted share, so the
# diagonal is a meaningful reference and the three panels are the same question about item, class
# and interaction rather than three different ones.
# The frame is `df`, not `d`: tibble() evaluates its arguments in order, so a column named `d`
# would shadow the frame for every argument after it.
.pair <- function(df, planted, measured, name) {
  # The planted share is taken over the three components only, leaving context out of the
  # denominator, because that is what the measured share divides too: context is averaged away in
  # forming the item-by-class means and cannot appear in them. Left unmatched the two axes divide
  # different things and the diagonal means nothing, since a faithful representation would sit
  # above it by however much context the language held. Taken this way both axes are the
  # component's share of the same three things and the diagonal is a faithful representation.
  # Dividing by the three rather than by one minus the context is also the safer arithmetic: the
  # four achieved shares sum to one only to within a percent, and this way the three always sum
  # to exactly one.
  tot <- df$ach_item + df$ach_class + df$ach_int
  ok <- !is.na(tot) & tot > 1e-3
  tibble(d = df$d[ok], component = name,
         planted = df[[planted]][ok] / tot[ok],
         measured = df[[measured]][ok])
}
.res <- toy_relu |> filter(resolved)
toy_learn <- bind_rows(
  .pair(.res, "ach_item", "size_item", "item"),
  .pair(.res, "ach_class", "size_class", "class"),
  .pair(.res, "ach_int", "size_interaction", "interaction")) |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, c("item", "class", "interaction")),
         bin = cut(planted, c(-Inf, .02, .06, .12, .22, .40, Inf))) |>
  filter(!is.na(planted), !is.na(measured))
# The binned summary stays for the prose; the figure draws the runs and a fit through them.
toy_learn_bin <- toy_learn |> group_by(component, d, bin) |>
  summarize(n = n(), x = median(planted), med = median(measured),
            lo = quantile(measured, .025), hi = quantile(measured, .975), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 10)

# The linear arm, prepared the same way, for the comparison the prose makes. It is not drawn in
# @fig-toy, which would double the lines for one sentence.
.lin <- toy |> filter(act == "linear", w_item > 0, w_class > 0) |>
  mutate(resolved = size_item_excludes_zero | size_class_excludes_zero |
                      size_interaction_excludes_zero) |>
  filter(resolved)
toy_learn_lin <- bind_rows(
  .pair(.lin, "ach_item", "size_item", "item"),
  .pair(.lin, "ach_class", "size_class", "class"),
  .pair(.lin, "ach_int", "size_interaction", "interaction")) |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, c("item", "class", "interaction"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(planted), !is.na(measured))

# Both arms in one frame for @fig-toy, which draws them as rows. toy_learn and toy_learn_lin are
# left alone: the prose indexes them separately.
toy_learn_both <- bind_rows(mutate(toy_learn, act = "ReLU"),
                            mutate(toy_learn_lin, act = "linear")) |>
  mutate(act = factor(act, c("ReLU", "linear")))

# Colour carries width here, since the components are separated by panel. A single ramp from the
# University of Oregon's green, because width is ordered and hues are not.
# Built from the data rather than written out, so that adding a width to the grid cannot
# silently drop its line for want of a color.
WIDC <- setNames(colorRampPalette(c("#BFCFA8", UO[["green"]]))(length(unique(toy$d))),
                 sort(unique(toy$d)))

# The fitted slope of represented share against the language's share, which is the quantity the
# prose quotes: how much of an increase in the language reaches the representation. Below one
# means the component is represented at less than its rate in the language.
slope <- function(dd, comp, dat = toy_learn) {
  x <- dat[dat$d == dd & dat$component == comp, ]
  unname(coef(stats::lm(measured ~ planted, data = x))[2])
}
slope_lin <- function(dd) slope(dd, "interaction", toy_learn_lin)

# The linear arm's composition by width, for the contrast the prose draws.
toy_comp_lin <- toy_learn_lin |> group_by(d, component) |>
  summarize(med = median(measured), .groups = "drop")
cmplin <- function(dd, comp) toy_comp_lin$med[toy_comp_lin$d == dd & toy_comp_lin$component == comp]

# Reproducibility at a FIXED language. Within a cell of weights, context weight and width the
# only thing that varies is the seed, so the spread across those runs is run-to-run variability.
# Spread pooled over languages is not: it is dominated by the languages differing, which is the
# horizontal axis of @fig-toy showing up on the vertical one.
toy_seed <- toy_relu |> filter(resolved) |>
  group_by(w_item, w_class, w_int, w_ctx, d) |>
  filter(dplyr::n() >= 3) |>
  summarize(item = max(size_item) - min(size_item),
            class = max(size_class) - min(size_class),
            interaction = max(size_interaction) - min(size_interaction), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(d) |>
  summarize(item = median(item), class = median(class),
            interaction = median(interaction), .groups = "drop")
seedspan <- function(dd, comp) toy_seed[[comp]][toy_seed$d == dd]

# Reach into the per-component view: the measured share at the lowest or highest planted band.
lrn <- function(dd, comp, top = TRUE) {
  x <- toy_learn_bin[toy_learn_bin$d == dd & toy_learn_bin$component == comp, ]
  x <- x[order(x$x), ]
  x$med[if (top) nrow(x) else 1]
}

# Pooled composition by width, for the prose.
toy_comp <- toy_long |> group_by(d, component) |>
  summarize(n = n(), med = median(share),
            lo = quantile(share, .025), hi = quantile(share, .975), .groups = "drop")

# Pooled over languages, for the prose and for the width trend on its own.
toy_width <- toy_long |> group_by(d, component) |>
  summarize(n = n(), med = median(share), lo = quantile(share, .025),
            hi = quantile(share, .975), .groups = "drop")
cmp <- function(dd, comp, col = "med") {
  toy_width[[col]][toy_width$d == dd & toy_width$component == comp]
}
cmpw <- function(dd, comp) cmp(dd, comp, "hi") - cmp(dd, comp, "lo")
unbuilt <- function(dd, col = "pct") toy_unbuilt[[col]][toy_unbuilt$d == dd]

# How the other properties of the language move the composition. Reported in the appendix rather
# than folded into the figure, so nothing is collapsed without saying so.
toy_bylang <- bind_rows(
  toy_relu |> filter(resolved) |>
    mutate(property = "context in the language",
           level = cut(ach_ctx, c(-Inf, .3, .7, Inf),
                       labels = c("under 30%", "30 to 70%", "over 70%"))),
  toy_relu |> filter(resolved) |>
    mutate(property = "item against class",
           level = cut(w_item / pmax(w_class, 1e-9), c(-Inf, .95, 1.05, Inf),
                       labels = c("item < class", "item = class", "item > class")))) |>
  group_by(property, level) |>
  summarize(runs = n(), item = median(size_item), class = median(size_class),
            interaction = median(size_interaction), .groups = "drop")

# Capacity: below 1 every component can have its own axis, above 1 they cannot.
# One overlap for a table: the value, how many times its own null's median it is, and how many of
# the measurements fall outside that null's 95% interval. The multiple is what makes overlaps
# comparable across widths, since the null moves by orders of magnitude with d; the count is what
# says the effect holds rather than resting on one measurement. Both tables use this, so they
# report the same three things and differ only in what a row is and how many measurements it holds.
# Per-model renderings, for tables whose rows are one model rather than six. These are the
# quantities as measured, with no median taken across models: a value with its own re-split
# interval, and an overlap with its own null's median. Vectorized, so they work inside mutate.
ci <- function(m, lo, hi, digits = 3) {
  f <- paste0("%.", digits, "f")
  out <- sprintf(paste0(f, " [", f, ", ", f, "]"), m, lo, hi)
  out[is.na(m)] <- "---"
  out
}
ov1 <- function(v, med, digits = 3) {
  out <- sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f (%.1f×)"), v, v / med)
  out[is.na(v)] <- "---"
  out
}

ov <- function(v, med, lo, hi, digits = 3) {
  m <- median(v, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (is.na(m)) return("---")
  ratio <- m / median(med, na.rm = TRUE)
  out <- sum(!is.na(v) & (v > hi | v < lo))
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f  (%.1f×, %d/%d)"), m, ratio, out, sum(!is.na(v)))
}

# One size for a table: the median share, and how many measurements clear zero -- their re-split
# 95% interval excludes zero. All three sizes are cross-split dot products with a null of exactly
# zero, so there is no "x null median" multiple to report and no raw null band to read against;
# `ez` is the per-measurement excludes-zero flag.
# A size as the share, with an interval when one is supplied, and how many of the group's
# measurements have a re-split interval clear of zero.
#
# What belongs in the brackets depends on what the row pools. Where a row is six models, the
# re-split interval is the wrong interval to print: it is 35 to 110 times narrower than the
# spread across those models, so it would claim the quantity is pinned to a thousandth while the
# models themselves disagree in the second decimal. The across-model range is the honest spread
# at that level. The re-split
# interval still does its work through the count, which is what says each model is clear of zero.
sz <- function(share, ez, lo = NULL, hi = NULL, digits = 3) {
  m <- median(share, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (is.na(m)) return("---")
  f <- paste0("%.", digits, "f")
  base <- if (is.null(lo)) sprintf(f, m) else
    sprintf(paste0(f, " [", f, ", ", f, "]"), m, lo, hi)
  n <- sum(!is.na(ez))
  if (n == 0) return(base)                                   # intervals not measured yet
  k <- sum(ez %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE"), na.rm = TRUE)
  sprintf("%s (%d/%d)", base, k, n)
}

# "4 of 6", or "NA" before the intervals are measured, for use in prose. For a size, "clearing"
# means its re-split 95% interval excludes zero.
outof <- function(constr, stem) {
  v <- llm_deep[[paste0(stem, "_excludes_zero")]][llm_deep$construction == constr]
  if (!length(v) || all(is.na(v))) return("NA")
  sprintf("%d of %d", sum(v %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE")), sum(!is.na(v)))
}

toy_cap <- toy |> filter(w_int > 0, w_item > 0, w_class > 0) |>
  # Same inclusion rule as @fig-toy: a run contributes only if at least one component's re-split
  # interval excludes zero, since otherwise the three shares divide noise.
  filter(size_item_excludes_zero | size_class_excludes_zero | size_interaction_excludes_zero) |>
  group_by(act, capacity) |>
  # Formatted here rather than in the table, because `ov` needs the runs themselves to count how
  # many fall outside their null; a summarized row no longer has them.
  summarize(n = n(), size_int = median(size_interaction),
            # median with the 95% range over the runs in the row. A row pools hundreds of runs
            # that differ in seed and in what was planted, and the median alone said nothing
            # about how much they differ.
            sz_int = sz(size_interaction, size_interaction_excludes_zero,
                        quantile(size_interaction, .025), quantile(size_interaction, .975),
                        digits = 3),
            ov_item = ov(leak_item_into_class, null_med, null_lo, null_hi, 4),
            ov_int = ov(leak_int_into_margins, null_int_med, null_int_lo, null_int, 3),
            overlap = median(leak_item_into_class, na.rm = TRUE),
            floor = median(null_hi, na.rm = TRUE),
            ratio = median(leak_item_into_class / null_hi, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

# Context is the nuisance dial: how much of the target is about something other than the item,
# the class and their conjunction. The high end is the regime Experiment 2 sits in.
toy_noise <- toy |> filter(w_int > 0, w_item > 0, w_class > 0) |>
  mutate(cbin = cut(ach_ctx, c(-Inf, .2, .5, .8, Inf),
                    labels = c("<20%", "20-50%", "50-80%", ">80%"))) |>
  group_by(act, cbin) |>
  summarize(n = n(), size_int = median(size_interaction),
            flagged_ez = mean(ez, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

g <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
cm <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")

# Short display names for the two constructions. The data keeps the long ones, which the prose
# and the inline expressions index by.
SHORT <- c("POS (noun/verb)"               = "part of speech",
           "role (subject/object)"         = "grammatical role")
shortname <- function(x) unname(SHORT[as.character(x)])
# The portable fraction of @tbl-posabl, for one model size with positions intact or zeroed,
# so the prose quotes the same numbers the table does rather than hardcoding them.
pf <- function(size, positions) {
  d <- rd("llm_unified_form.csv") |>
    filter(grepl(size, model, fixed = TRUE), grepl("^pretrained", init)) |>
    mutate(pos = ifelse(grepl("noposemb$", init), "zeroed", "intact")) |>
    filter(pos == positions) |>
    slice_max(layer, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
  g(d$std_size_class / (d$std_size_class + d$std_size_interaction), 3)
}

capget <- function(a, cap, col) toy_cap[[col]][toy_cap$act == a & toy_cap$capacity == cap]

# ---- Experiment 1: the component models ----------------------------------------------------
# Written by scripts/toy/prepare_results.R from the fitted models, which are ~200MB each and stay
# out of git, so every number the prose quotes comes from the fit without the fit being present.
rcoef <- rd("results_coefficients.csv")
rcrwd <- rd("results_contrasts.csv")
rdiag <- rd("results_diagnostics.csv")
rpred <- rd("results_predictions.csv")

# One coefficient, as the prose quotes it: estimate with its 95% credible interval.
cf <- function(comp, lab, armv = "relu", kindv = "size", dig = 3) {
  r <- rcoef[rcoef$component == comp & rcoef$label == lab &
             rcoef$arm == armv & rcoef$kind == kindv, ]
  sprintf("%+.*f [%+.*f, %+.*f]", dig, r$estimate, dig, r$lo95, dig, r$hi95)
}

# The same coefficient for running prose: the estimate alone. Whether the interval clears zero is
# said in words, and the interval itself is in the appendix tables, where a reader can see it
# beside every other term of the same model rather than the one the sentence happens to quote.
# What the measure reports where the language holds NO interaction at all: the level a learner
# registers when there is nothing to register. Quoted by width, because it is not constant.
.add <- function(w, armv) {
  cv <- toy$converged %in% c(TRUE, "True", "TRUE")
  toy[toy$w_int == 0 & toy$act == armv & toy$d == w & cv, ]
}
addint  <- function(w, armv = "ReLU", dig = 4) g(median(.add(w, armv)$size_interaction, na.rm = TRUE), dig)
addflag <- function(w, armv = "ReLU") sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(.add(w, armv)$ez, na.rm = TRUE))

# Overlap at the deepest layer as a multiple of its own chance level, across models and categories.
ovr <- function(col = "leak", dig = 1) {
  v <- llm_deep[[col]] / llm_deep[[paste0(col, "_null_med")]]
  v <- v[is.finite(v)]
  sprintf("%s to %s", g(min(v), dig), g(max(v), dig))
}

# How closely the learners reproduce the language: cross-entropy at convergence minus the entropy
# of the target, which is the Kullback-Leibler divergence to the truth. Quoted so the shares are
# read as how a representation is organised, not as how much of the language was learned.
kl <- function(w, armv = "ReLU", dig = 4) {
  cv <- toy$converged %in% c(TRUE, "True", "TRUE")
  g(median(toy$fit_gap[toy$act == armv & toy$d == w & cv], na.rm = TRUE), dig)
}

b <- function(comp, lab, armv = "relu", kindv = "size", dig = 3) {
  r <- rcoef[rcoef$component == comp & rcoef$label == lab &
             rcoef$arm == armv & rcoef$kind == kindv, ]
  sprintf("$\\beta = %+.*f$", dig, r$estimate)
}

# A fitted share at one width, from the grid that holds effect sizes at their means.
# The overlap models are fitted on the log of the ratio to chance, so those fitted values are
# exponentiated back to the multiple of chance the prose quotes. The size models are already on
# the share scale.
fv <- function(comp, w, armv = "relu", kindv = "size", dig = 2) {
  r <- rpred[rpred$component == comp & rpred$width == w & rpred$arm == armv &
             rpred$kind == kindv & rpred$grid == "arch", ]
  v <- median(r$epred)
  g(if (kindv == "overlap") exp(v) else v, dig)
}

# ---- Experiment 2: language model representations ----
# Per-class token medians, from the per-item stimulus list rather than the pooled summary. A
# single pooled median cannot say whether a form occurs that often in EACH class or that often in
# total; both are reported instead, in the order of the contrast. The counts are corpus-level and
# identical across all six models, so one model gives the figure.
stim <- rd("stimuli_items.csv")
# The span of those per-class medians, for prose, where a slash pair does not read as a sentence.
stimrange <- function() {
  v <- unlist(lapply(c("pos_noun_verb_form", "role_nsubj_obj"), function(k) {
    g <- stim[stim$construction == k, ]
    g <- g[g$model == g$model[1], ]
    c(median(g$n_class_a), median(g$n_class_b))
  }))
  sprintf("%.0f to %.0f", min(v), max(v))
}
stimmed <- function(key) {
  g <- stim[stim$construction == key, ]
  g <- g[g$model == g$model[1], ]
  sprintf("%.0f / %.0f", median(g$n_class_a), median(g$n_class_b))
}

grid_stats <- rd("methods_grid_stats.csv")
gs <- function(constr, col) {
  v <- grid_stats[[col]][grid_stats$construction == constr]
  # median(numeric(0)) is NA, so a construction missing from the stats file used to reach the
  # rendered PDF as a silent "NA". Refuse to render instead.
  if (!length(v)) stop("methods_grid_stats.csv has no rows for construction '", constr,
                       "'; regenerate it with scripts/llm/dataset_stats.py", call. = FALSE)
  if (is.numeric(v)) round(median(v)) else v[1]
}

# The same, but falling back to the last typed value rather than stopping the render, for
# construction keys the stats file only grows on its next regeneration (the role and
# form-keyed POS rows and the corpus counts). Once the stats file carries the key, the data
# wins and the fallback is dead weight.
gsf <- function(constr, col, fallback = NA_real_) {
  v <- grid_stats[[col]][grid_stats$construction == constr]
  v <- v[!is.na(v)]
  if (!length(v)) return(fallback)
  if (is.numeric(v)) round(median(v)) else v[1]
}

# Deepest-layer medians, so the prose cannot drift from the table: every figure quoted in the
# text is read from here rather than typed in. `ld` is the median across models.
llm_deep <- NULL   # filled once `llm` exists, below
ld <- function(constr, col) median(llm_deep[[col]][llm_deep$construction == constr], na.rm = TRUE)
# Same, at the embedding layer, and a range of either across the two constructions. Both read
# NA through rather than erroring, so a column the CSVs predate degrades to a blank in the text.
l0 <- function(constr, col) median(llm[[col]][llm$construction == constr & llm$layer == 0],
                                   na.rm = TRUE)
# A size as a share of the whole representation rather than of the grid: the grid's share of the
# total, times the component's share of the item-by-class structure.
tot <- function(constr, col) ld(constr, col) * ld(constr, "between_adj")

# Range of a column across every category and model at one depth (embeddings, or deepest),
# for prose that quotes a spread over all twelve grids rather than one construction's medians.
allrange <- function(col, deep = TRUE, digits = 4) {
  d <- if (deep) llm_deep else llm[llm$layer == 0, ]
  v <- d[[col]]; v <- v[!is.na(v)]
  sprintf("%s to %s", g(min(v), digits), g(max(v), digits))
}

rng <- function(f, col, digits = 2) {
  v <- vapply(levels(llm_deep$construction), function(k) f(k, col), numeric(1))
  if (all(is.na(v))) return("NA")
  paste0(g(min(v, na.rm = TRUE), digits), " to ", g(max(v, na.rm = TRUE), digits))
}

# The range of a column across the six models at one construction's deepest layer, for the
# few places the prose quotes a spread rather than a median. Same NA-through convention.
# deep = FALSE reads the embedding layer instead, which is where the keying comparison lives.
ldrng <- function(constr, col, digits = 4, deep = TRUE) {
  d <- if (deep) llm_deep else llm[llm$layer == 0, ]
  v <- d[[col]][d$construction == constr]
  if (all(is.na(v))) return("NA")
  sprintf("%s to %s", g(min(v, na.rm = TRUE), digits), g(max(v, na.rm = TRUE), digits))
}

# `scale` pairs the two families at the three matched widths, so a figure can separate the six
# models with three linetypes and two colors rather than leaving three of them on one color.
MODELS <- tibble::tribble(
  ~model,                                       ~family,  ~size,  ~scale,
  "znhoughton/opt-babylm-125m-20eps-seed964",   "BabyLM", "125M", "125M/160M",
  "znhoughton/opt-babylm-350m-20eps-seed964",   "BabyLM", "350M", "350M/410M",
  "znhoughton/opt-babylm-1.3B-20eps-seed964",   "BabyLM", "1.3B", "1.3B/1.4B",
  "EleutherAI/pythia-160m",                     "Pythia", "160M", "125M/160M",
  "EleutherAI/pythia-410m",                     "Pythia", "410M", "350M/410M",
  "EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b",                     "Pythia", "1.4B", "1.3B/1.4B") |>
  dplyr::mutate(scale = factor(scale, c("125M/160M", "350M/410M", "1.3B/1.4B")))

# The three same-token constructions carried in the body. Each file reports the same measure;
# the POS file prefixes its columns std_ because it also stores an unstandardized read.
# POS is read from the SURFACE-FORM-keyed run. Keyed on the lemma instead, an item pools every
# inflected form (run/runs as a noun against run/runs/ran/running as a verb), which are
# different tokens, and the static embedding layer separates them: the layer-0 interaction is
# 0.083-0.172 keyed on the lemma against 0.0010-0.0028 keyed on the form, a 50-100x difference
# that is inflectional rather than representational. The file also holds random-init rows, which
# the paper makes no claim about -- these are endpoint measurements -- so they are filtered out.
# These carry the orientation nulls and the between-grid share. They also hold the random and
# position-ablated inits, so all three sources need the pretrained filter.
llm <- bind_rows(
  rd("llm_unified_form.csv") |>
    ensure("std_size_item_ci_med", "std_size_class_ci_med", "std_size_interaction_ci_med", "std_between_share_adj", "std_obs_size_class", "std_size_class_excludes_zero", "std_obs_size_interaction", "std_size_interaction_excludes_zero", "std_obs_size_item", "std_size_item_excludes_zero") |>
    filter(init == "pretrained") |>
    transmute(model, layer, d, n_items = std_n_items, construction = "POS (noun/verb)",
              size_item = std_size_item, size_class = std_size_class,
              size_int = std_size_interaction,
              leak = std_leak_item_into_class, leak_int = std_leak_int_into_margins,
              leak_null = std_leak_item_into_class_null_hi,
              leak_null_lo = std_leak_item_into_class_null_lo,
              leak_null_med = std_leak_item_into_class_null_med,
              leak_int_null = std_leak_int_into_margins_null_hi,
              leak_int_null_lo = std_leak_int_into_margins_null_lo,
              leak_int_null_med = std_leak_int_into_margins_null_med,
              between = std_between_share, between_adj = std_between_share_adj,
              between_var = std_between_var, within_var = std_within_var,
              obs_size_class = std_obs_size_class,
              size_class_excludes_zero = std_size_class_excludes_zero,
              obs_size_interaction = std_obs_size_interaction,
              size_interaction_excludes_zero = std_size_interaction_excludes_zero,
              obs_size_item = std_obs_size_item,
              size_item_excludes_zero = std_size_item_excludes_zero,
              size_item_ci_lo = std_size_item_ci_lo, size_item_ci_med = std_size_item_ci_med,
              size_item_ci_hi = std_size_item_ci_hi,
              size_class_ci_lo = std_size_class_ci_lo, size_class_ci_med = std_size_class_ci_med,
              size_class_ci_hi = std_size_class_ci_hi,
              size_interaction_ci_lo = std_size_interaction_ci_lo,
              size_interaction_ci_med = std_size_interaction_ci_med,
              size_interaction_ci_hi = std_size_interaction_ci_hi),
  rd("llm_role.csv") |>
    ensure("size_item_ci_med", "size_class_ci_med", "size_interaction_ci_med", "between_share_adj", "obs_size_class", "size_class_excludes_zero", "obs_size_interaction", "size_interaction_excludes_zero", "obs_size_item", "size_item_excludes_zero") |>
    filter(init == "pretrained") |>
    transmute(model, layer, d, n_items, construction = "role (subject/object)",
              size_item, size_class, size_int = size_interaction,
              leak = leak_item_into_class,
              leak_int = leak_int_into_margins,
              leak_null = leak_item_into_class_null_hi,
              leak_null_lo = leak_item_into_class_null_lo,
              leak_null_med = leak_item_into_class_null_med,
              leak_int_null = leak_int_into_margins_null_hi,
              leak_int_null_lo = leak_int_into_margins_null_lo,
              leak_int_null_med = leak_int_into_margins_null_med,
              between = between_share, between_adj = between_share_adj,
              between_var = between_var, within_var = within_var,
              obs_size_class = obs_size_class,
              size_class_excludes_zero = size_class_excludes_zero,
              obs_size_interaction = obs_size_interaction,
              size_interaction_excludes_zero = size_interaction_excludes_zero,
              obs_size_item = obs_size_item,
              size_item_excludes_zero = size_item_excludes_zero,
              size_item_ci_lo, size_item_ci_med, size_item_ci_hi,
              size_class_ci_lo, size_class_ci_med, size_class_ci_hi,
              size_interaction_ci_lo, size_interaction_ci_med, size_interaction_ci_hi)) |>
  left_join(MODELS, by = "model") |>
  mutate(construction = factor(construction, c("POS (noun/verb)", "role (subject/object)")),
         depth = layer / ave(layer, model, construction, FUN = max),  # 0 = embeddings, 1 = final
         # Sizes are shares of the re-split medians, not of the permutation-denoised single
         # split. The cross-split product already has a null of exactly zero, so the permutation
         # baseline was subtracting an estimate of nothing, and it was subtracted from the item
         # and interaction but not from the class, which left the three on different footings.
         # The medians carry no permutation at all and are on the same scale as the intervals
         # quoted beside them, so a share and its interval are finally the same quantity.
         sz_denom = size_item_ci_med + size_class_ci_med + size_interaction_ci_med,
         size_item = size_item_ci_med / sz_denom,
         size_class = size_class_ci_med / sz_denom,
         size_int = size_interaction_ci_med / sz_denom,
         size_item_lo = size_item_ci_lo / sz_denom,
         size_item_hi = size_item_ci_hi / sz_denom,
         size_class_lo = size_class_ci_lo / sz_denom,
         size_class_hi = size_class_ci_hi / sz_denom,
         size_int_lo = size_interaction_ci_lo / sz_denom,
         size_int_hi = size_interaction_ci_hi / sz_denom)

llm_deep <- llm |> group_by(construction, model) |> filter(layer == max(layer)) |> ungroup()

# The same measure applied after the unembedding as well as at the final hidden layer, on
# identical tokens, written by scripts/llm/measure_output_layer.py. Both members of a pair are
# point estimates from one run, which is what makes them comparable to each other and what puts
# them about 0.003 from the re-split medians `llm` carries.
outl <- rd("llm_output_layer.csv") |>
  mutate(where = factor(where, c("hidden", "output")))

# A construction measured on fewer than six models would silently report a median over whatever
# happened to finish, so say so loudly instead.
local({
  n <- table(droplevels(llm_deep$construction))
  if (any(n < 6)) warning("under-covered constructions: ",
                          paste(names(n)[n < 6], n[n < 6], sep = "=", collapse = ", "),
                          call. = FALSE)
})

# ---- Effect size on a scale a reader can interpret ------------------------------------------
# A share of the item-by-class grid says how the structure between words and classes divides; it does not say
# how much of an actual token's representation any of it accounts for, and the two differ by
# roughly a factor of three because most of a token's variation is context within its own word and class.
# These put the three components in one currency: the reduction in squared error when predicting
# a token's hidden state, against guessing the grand mean. The components are orthogonal by
# construction, so each contributes its own variance term and the ladder is cumulative. The
# sizes already sum to one, so a component's variance is its share times the total structure
# between words and classes; `gi` is the interaction's gain over the ADDITIVE model rather than over the mean,
# which is the quantity the additive account is being judged on.
llm_gain <- llm_deep |>
  mutate(v_item = size_item * between_var, v_class = size_class * between_var,
         v_int = size_int * between_var, tot_var = between_var + within_var,
         ga = v_item / tot_var,                      # know the word
         gb = v_class / tot_var,                     # know the class
         gab = (v_item + v_class) / tot_var,         # know both: the additive account
         gabg = (v_item + v_class + v_int) / tot_var,# know both plus the interaction
         gg = v_int / tot_var,                       # what the interaction adds, same scale
         gi = v_int / (v_int + within_var),          # ... as a share of what additive leaves
         gctx = within_var / tot_var)                # the rest: context within a word and class

# A gain as a percentage range across the twelve grids, or across one construction's six models.
gr <- function(col, constr = NULL, digits = 0) {
  d <- if (is.null(constr)) llm_gain else llm_gain[llm_gain$construction == constr, ]
  v <- 100 * d[[col]]
  sprintf("%s%% to %s%%", g(min(v), digits), g(max(v), digits))
}
# How many of the twelve grids have the interaction contributing at least as much as the class.
gbeat <- function() sum(llm_gain$gg >= llm_gain$gb)
```

# Introduction

Lexical representations are deceptively complex: a single word can carry vastly different meanings depending on the context, yet these meanings remain recognizably related. The categorization literature has long recognized this tension, noting that assigning an instance to a specific category is rarely straightforward. Simple rule-based approaches quickly break down: a three-legged cat is undeniably a cat, even if it violates one of the criteria used to define the category. Ultimately, defining a lexical category in precise terms may be impossible. Yet, as U.S. Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart famously observed, we may not be able to define a category precisely, but we nevertheless "know it when \[we\] see it."[^1]

[^1]: In *Jacobellis v. Ohio* (1964), Justice Stewart famously addressed the difficulty of defining obscenity, remarking that while he may not be able to formulate a precise definition, he could still recognize obscene material when he saw it.

This central tradeoff between the context-specificity and the generalizability of linguistic representations has fueled long-standing debates over the nature of lexical representations [@goldinger1998echoes; @mcqueen2006phonological; @pierrehumbert2016phonological; @kapatsinski2010whatisit]. A substantial body of work suggests that linguistic representations contain both abstract, generalizable information as well as information specific to particular experiences [@goldinger1998echoes; @mcqueen2006phonological; @pierrehumbert2016phonological; @kapatsinski2010whatisit]. For example, children can generalize a productive morphological pattern to forms they have never encountered before [@berkoChildsLearningEnglish1958], while lexical representations can preserve fine-grained information about particular words, phrases, and contexts [@goldinger1998echoes; @palmeri1993episodicencoding; @bybee1999usagebasedphonology]. Thus, there is little controversy that linguistic knowledge can contain both generalizable and item-specific information. The more fundamental question for the present study is how widespread item-specific information is, and whether it is present even when there is no item-specific information in the input that requires it.

## Item-Specificity in Linguistic Representations

Over the last few decades, a great deal of evidence has accumulated showing that linguistic representations are not as decomposable into abstract parts as was traditionally thought. Much of the evidence for this comes from the phonetics literature, showing that phonetic representations are surprisingly rich [@goldinger1998echoes; @palmeri1993episodicencoding], as well as the psycholinguistic literature's line of research demonstrating the holistic storage of multi-morphemic and multi-word phrases [@bybee1999usagebasedphonology; @houghton2025roleabstractrepresentations; @houghton2026holisticstorageverb+up; @houghton2023doespredictabilitydrive; @stembergerAreInflectedForms2004; @stembergerFrequencyLexicalStorage1986].

The strongest evidence for context-specific storage comes from frequency in favorable context effects [FFC, @raymondBrown2012frequency; see @kapatsinski2026lexicalfrequency for a review]. FFC effects describe a phenomenon in which a form's behavior is predicted by how often it has occurred in a context that conditions a change rather than by how often it has occurred overall. FFC effects show that it is not raw frequency, but rather frequency in a specific context, that is stored. For example, @raymondBrownHealy2016cumulative found that English words ending in /t/ or /d/ were more likely to be deleted if they were words that frequently occurred before a consonant, the conditioning context for that deletion, regardless of the word's overall frequency. Crucially, this deletion was observed even when the word occurred outside the conditioning context [@bybee2002wordfrequency]. While we consider FFC effects to be the clearest evidence for context-specific storage, they are by no means the only evidence: context-specific storage is also evidenced by word-specific patterns of phonetic reduction [@bybeeScheibman1999constituency], the persistence of subphonemic phonetic detail in memory [@mcmurrayGradientSensitivityWithincategory2008; @palmeri1993episodicencoding; @miller1994internalstructure], phrase-specific influences on reading times [@siyanova-chanturia2011seeingphrasetime], lexically specific word-order preferences [@morgan2016abstractknowledgedirect; @morganModelingIdiosyncraticPreferences2015; @morgan2024productiveknowledgeitemspecific], and phrasal frequency effects on the recognition of their component units [@kapatsinskiRadicke2009prefabs; @houghton2025multiwordrepresentationsminds].

These findings establish that linguistic representations can encode information specific to particular words and contexts, but they do not tell us how widespread such information is. Consider *walk*, which can function as both a noun and a verb. If its representation as a verb was fully determined by a representation of *walk* and a representation of the verb category, then nothing in its representation would be specific to the *walk*-verb combination. If, instead, *walk* as a verb had a representation of its own, that representation would contain information that cannot be reduced to its constituent parts. Word embeddings offer a way of asking this directly, since they give a separate representation of a word in each category it occurs in. Recent work has targeted a version of this question and demonstrated that abstractions can be narrower than might be expected [@shafaeiBajestan2024pluralization; @nikolaev2025casenumber], but such narrowness still reflects information shared across words within a specific class, just one that is narrower than the classes traditionally proposed. What remains unclear is whether individual word-category combinations have representations of their own.

## Storage Without Idiosyncracy

There is little doubt that idiosyncratic words or phrases, such as idioms, must be stored in some form, since their properties are not reducible to those of their individual component parts. However, it is less clear to what extent forms that could in principle be represented compositionally (i.e., fully regular forms) are, in fact, represented compositionally.

Usage-based theories have argued that even regular forms are stored holistically as a function of usage. Bybee [@bybee2001] and later Goldberg [@goldberg2019explain] have proposed that frequent words and phrases can be stored even when their properties are fully predictable. From this view, storage need not be a consequence of idiosyncrasy. In fact, it has even been argued that storage is a prerequisite to a representation becoming idiosyncratic [@bybee2001; @goldberg2019explain].

These debates about the nature of lexical representations create an important distinction between two possibilities. If item-specific representations arise primarily because linguistic forms are idiosyncratic, then regular forms should not necessarily have representations of their own. If frequent regular forms are stored even in the absence of idiosyncratic information, however, item-specific representations should be detectable even when the input provides no idiosyncratic information that requires them.

## Present study

The present study asks how item-specific information is represented and how widespread it is. We focus on representations of words in grammatical classes and decompose a word-in-class representation into three components: a class component (e.g., a verb component), an item component (e.g., *walk* regardless of the part of speech), and an item-of-a-specific-class component (e.g., *walk* as a verb).

These questions are difficult to settle behaviorally, since a learner with no item-specific representations can look like one that has them [@houghton2026exemplars]. The question is fundamentally about the structure of a representation, and unlike in humans, model representations can be examined directly [@pluthInterpretabilityWhisperEncodings2026; @hinton1986distributed; @elhage2022superposition]. This makes neural network models a useful setting in which to ask what properties of the input give rise to item-specific representations. In particular, do such representations emerge only when a form has item-specific properties, or can they also arise for forms whose properties are fully predictable from their constituent parts?

We first validate this decomposition on an artificial language in which we independently control the amount of information associated with the item, the class, and their interaction. This allows us to ask how a learner represents genuinely item-specific information when it is present in the input, and whether item-specific structure appears even when no interaction is present in the input. We then apply the same decomposition to six pretrained language models across two linguistic constructions to ask how much item-specific information is present in naturally occurring linguistic representations.

Our main contributions are as follows:

-   We introduce a method for decomposing word-in-context representations into lexical, grammatical, and word-class components, and validate it on an artificial language.

-   Across six pretrained models, the word-class component is consistently present and grows with depth; in the artificial language its size is governed more by representational capacity than by the language's composition. The lexical and grammatical components are nearly orthogonal, while the word-class component overlaps with both.

-   We show that the word-class component contains information about the class itself beyond the shared class representation.

# Experiment 1: Artificial Languages {#sec-exp1}

In Experiment 1 we test our measurement on an artificial language whose features we control. This allows us to validate our measurement while simultaneously examining how different features of the language affect a model's representations.

## Dataset {#sec-exp1-data}

In order to examine the separability of linguistic representations, we constructed an artificial language which comprises a probability distribution over a vocabulary of `r cm(600)` tokens. Every observation is a combination of a **form** (one of `r max(toy$n_form)`), a **class** (one of `r max(toy$n_class)`), and a **context** (drawn from a pool of 400). The motivation for this setup is to give each word a naturalistic environment: each word occurs in a context that favors a specific class-membership (e.g., *walk* as a verb occurs in a different context than *walk* as a noun). Each form is observed `r max(toy$n_obs)` times in each class, each time in a different context, mirroring the patterns of human language. Consider *walk* used as a verb in one of those contexts. Four things determine the distribution over the next token. *Walk* itself contributes the same amount regardless of the class it is used in, and the verb class also contributes the same amount for every item. The third contribution is what is specific to *walk*-as-a-verb over and above those two: each pairing of a form with a class has its own random vector, drawn independently of the first two and then centered across forms and across classes, so that nothing in it can be attributed to *walk* alone or to the verb class alone. The context contributes the rest, which is noise as far as our question goes, though the model still has to encode it in order to accurately learn the language. The four are weighted, summed and passed through a softmax layer in order to create the ground truth probability distribution over next tokens for a given input:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&P(\text{next token} \mid f, c, x) = \\
&\quad \operatorname{softmax}\Big( s\big[\, w_\alpha\,\text{item}(f)
  + w_\beta\,\text{class}(c) \\
&\qquad + w_\gamma\,\text{int}(f,c)
  + w_{\text{ctx}}\,\text{context}(x) \,\big] \Big)
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-toy}

Each term is isotropically scaled to unit variance before being weighted,[^2] so changing the weights changes the mix of the three effects without changing how much signal there is in total; the constant $s = 3$ then scales that sum before the softmax, setting how peaked the resulting distribution is.

[^2]: Specifically, each observation consists of a form in a specific class and a context, paired with that term's contribution to the next-token distribution for that observation. We normalize this dataset by dividing each value by the total standard deviation across all observations.

The weights $w_\alpha$, $w_\beta$, and $w_\gamma$ in @eq-toy control how much of the true distribution each of the three effects contributes, and we cross them factorially over $\{0, 0.5, 1, 2\}$: zero removes an effect from the language altogether, and the other three values make an effect half as strong as another, equal to it, or twice it. Similarly, $w_{\text{ctx}}$ governs how much the context contributes, so we cross those languages with three context weights: $\{0.5, 2.0, 6.0\}$, ranging from context being a minor part of the true distribution to the dominant one. The four weights are subsequently rescaled together to unit length, such that $w_\alpha^2 + w_\beta^2 + w_\gamma^2 + w_{\text{ctx}}^2 = 1$.[^3] The ranks of the item and class are held fixed at `r unique(toy$r_item)` and `r unique(toy$r_class)` respectively but each language is crossed with four interaction effect ranks: $\{4, 16, 64, 177\}$, the highest of which is the ceiling that centering imposes ($(60-1)(4-1) = 177$). Additionally, we train a model on each of the resulting languages at hidden widths of `r paste(sort(unique(toy$d)), collapse = ", ")`, with either a linear or a ReLU activation. Each model is trained with the Adam optimizer at a learning rate of 0.01, with early stopping.[^conv] The whole grid is then run with five random seeds giving `r format(nrow(toy), big.mark = ",")` runs in all, of which `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(toy$converged))` trained to convergence. Full training details are listed in Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-grid}.

[^3]: This makes the resulting languages more comparable by enforcing the same total signal (i.e., the variance of the weighted sum in @eq-toy is held constant), despite individual differences in the amount that each individual term contributes.

[^conv]: A run counts as converged when the cross-entropy fails to improve by more than $10^{-5}$ over 40 consecutive iterations; runs still improving after 3,000 iterations are recorded as not converged. Stopping never depends on anything derived from the measurement, so it cannot bias the components we report.

## Method {#sec-exp1-method}

### The learner

The learner model is a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a single hidden layer of width $d$ and either a linear or a ReLU activation function.`\codefootnote{}`{=latex} The model takes as its input three pieces of information: form, class, and context. Each has its own embedding, and the three are concatenated and passed through the model which then outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary (@fig-training). The training objective is thus to minimize cross-entropy between the model's predicted distribution over the vocabulary and the exact ground-truth distribution.

![Structure of our model. Every form is observed 24 times at each class, each time in a different context; that variation across contexts is what the measurement later splits in two.](fig-training.pdf){#fig-training width="100%" fig-env="figure*"}

### Decomposing a representation {#sec-measure}

In order to measure the item-specific part of the representation, we decompose a word-in-context representation into a lexical component, a class component, and an idiosyncratic component. In Experiment 1, the representation we decompose is the MLP's hidden layer representation. Let $M[i,c] \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be the mean of those hidden states for item $i$ used at class $c$ (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-math}). We decompose those item-by-class means by centering, so that:

$$
M[i,c] \;=\; \mu + \alpha(i) + \beta(c) + \gamma(i,c),
$$ {#eq-decomp}

where $\mu$ is the grand mean; $\alpha(i)$ is item $i$'s mean across classes minus $\mu$, which conceptually is the representation unique to the item; $\beta(c)$ is the mean across items at class $c$ minus $\mu$, which conceptually is the representation unique to the class (e.g., noun vs verb); and $\gamma(i,c)$ is what item $i$ at class $c$ holds that neither marginal accounts for, which conceptually is the item-specific representation in a specific class (@fig-measurement). Each representation for a given item in a given class is exactly the sum of the four terms of @eq-decomp and no two of them vary together across those representations, so the squared lengths of each term (excluding $\mu$) sum to the total and we report each as a share.

Each of these averages is taken over a sample of observations that differ only in context, so each carries some of the context term of @eq-toy as noise. We remove it by dividing the observations into two evenly sized splits, running the decomposition on each split separately, and estimating each component's size as the dot product of its two split estimates, which is large when the splits agree about the component and near zero when they do not. As a result, noise that differs between the splits is independent and cancels.

For each representation we report two measurements. The first, which we call the *size* of a component, is the fraction of the representation accounted for by lexical, class, and idiosyncratic information: each component's squared length, summed over its vectors and divided by the total, so that the three fractions sum to one. The second, the *overlap* between components, quantifies the extent to which they occupy the same geometric directions. Specifically, we project the item vectors onto the class direction and record the fraction of their squared length that survives, and we project the interaction onto the smallest subspace containing both the item and the class vectors (i.e., the span of the two subspaces).[^4]

[^4]: The class effect spans at most one direction fewer than the number of classes, so it is low-dimensional in both experiments: one direction in Experiment 2 and at most three in Experiment 1. Its projection into the item subspace, which has many more dimensions, has high overlap by chance; we therefore do not report it.

To quantify whether a size is meaningful, we redraw the split two hundred times and estimate how often its confidence interval excludes zero; for components whose value is exactly zero this flags an effect about 5% of the time (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate}), the false-positive rate expected of a 95% confidence interval.

To quantify whether an overlap is meaningful, we project the effect, held exactly as measured, onto two hundred random subspaces of the same rank, which gives the distribution of overlaps an unrelated subspace would yield. An overlap below that baseline indicates meaningful orthogonality; an overlap above the baseline indicates meaningful non-orthogonality. We report each overlap as a multiple of the baseline's median, with how many measurements fall outside its 95% interval.

![The four item-by-class means formed by two items in two classes. The arrow is $\gamma(i,c)$.](fig-measurement.pdf){#fig-measurement width="78%"}

It's important to note that the weights in @eq-toy describe the ground-truth distribution the model is trained to match, while the measure decomposes the representation that the model *learns*, so the two sets of numbers are not necessarily analogous: a learner handed a language that is 85% interaction can learn a representation in which the interaction is far smaller (or larger). Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate} reports a separate check in which components were set directly in a representation and recovered almost exactly, which is what licenses interpreting the results below as facts about the learner rather than about the measure. We include runs only if at least one of the three components has a re-split interval excluding zero; where none does, the three shares divide noise.

### Analysis {#sec-exp1-analysis}

We model our data using an ordered beta regression [@kubinec2023ordbeta] for the sizes and a Gaussian model for the overlaps, both in *brms* [@burkner2017brms] with weakly informative priors, given in Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-grid}. For the sizes we fit a single model over all three components (@eq-ordbeta): a component's fraction of the representation is predicted by all three planted effect sizes, the hidden width, and the total rank of the planted structure, which is the item, class and interaction ranks summed (`r min(toy$rank)` to `r max(toy$rank)` across the grid), with every term crossed with component so that the architecture effects are free to differ between the item, the class and the interaction. All predictors are centered. A language here is one combination of the four weights and the interaction rank, `r cm(length(unique(paste(toy$key, toy$r_int))))` in all; the five seeds for a language are re-realizations of the same specification rather than different languages, so they share an intercept. Width is the only predictor that varies within a language, and so the only one that can carry a random slope: the effect sizes and the rank are properties of the language itself and are constant across its runs. A random intercept by run lets the three components measured from one trained model covary.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text{Share} \sim \text{Component} * \big( \text{ItemEffect} \\ & \quad + \text{ClassEffect} + \text{InteractionEffect} \\ & \quad + \text{log2(Width)} * \text{log2(TotalRank)} \big) \\ & \quad + (1 + \text{log2(Width)} \mid \text{Language}) \\ & \quad + (1 \mid \text{Run})
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ordbeta}

For the overlaps we likewise fit one model over both overlap measures, each expressed as a logged multiple of its own chance level, with the same crossing and the same random-effects structure (@eq-overlap). Coefficient values here indicate the extent to which each parameter causes the item, class, and interaction dimensions to be orthogonal or non-orthogonal.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text{log(Overlap/Chance)} \sim \text{Measure} * \big( \text{ItemEffect} \\ & \quad + \text{ClassEffect} + \text{InteractionEffect} \\ & \quad + \text{log2(Width)} * \text{log2(TotalRank)} \big) \\ & \quad + (1 + \text{log2(Width)} \mid \text{Language}) \\ & \quad + (1 \mid \text{Run})
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-overlap}

## Results {#sec-exp1-results}

Results are visualized in @fig-toy, with the full coefficient results included in Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-capacity}. Where the hidden layer is wide enough, the learners reproduce the language closely (median Kullback-Leibler divergence of `r kl(max(toy$d))` at the widest, against `r kl(min(toy$d))` at the narrowest; @fig-toy-fit reports the fit across the whole grid). The shares below therefore say what proportion of the representation each component accounts for, not how much of the language the model captured: the hidden layer has to carry each component in some form a linear readout can combine into the output distribution, not in the language's proportions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-toy
#| fig-width: 3.05
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Ground-truth effect size of each component in the language (x) against its size in the MLP's representations (y). Points are runs; lines are fitted values from @eq-ordbeta with 95% intervals, colored by hidden width."
#|
.fit <- rpred |>
  filter(kind == "size", grid == "planted") |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, c("item", "class", "interaction")),
         act = factor(arm, c("relu", "linear"), c("ReLU", "linear")))
ggplot(toy_learn_both, aes(planted, measured, color = factor(d), fill = factor(d))) +
  geom_point(size = .18, alpha = .14, stroke = 0) +
  geom_ribbon(data = .fit, aes(x = own, y = epred, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = factor(width)),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = .16) +
  geom_line(data = .fit, aes(x = own, y = epred, color = factor(width)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = .55) +
  facet_grid(act ~ component) +
  scale_color_manual(values = WIDC, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = WIDC, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, .5, 1),
                     labels = c("0", ".5", "1")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, .5, 1), labels = c("0", ".5", "1")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "effect size in the language", y = "effect size in the representation") +
  theme_paper(7) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.margin = margin(0, 0, -6, 0),
        legend.key.width = unit(10, "pt"), panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1))
```

Unsurprisingly, the effect size for each component increases as a function of the size of the effect planted in the language (and since the three components sum to 1, the other 2 components definitionally decrease). Of the three components, the item effect is strongest across every width (@fig-toy).

The size of the interaction barely depends on its rank on its own (`r b("interaction", "rank")`), which is by design: the interaction is scaled to the same variance at every rank, so raising its rank spreads it over more directions rather than making it larger. What governs how much of the interaction is encoded is the width of the hidden layer (`r b("interaction", "width")`). Rank enters by changing how much that width recovers (`r b("interaction", "width x rank")`): at narrow widths a higher-rank interaction needs more directions than the layer has and the excess is lost, while once the layer is wide enough the model represents more of it, and does. This is not the case for the item effect, which decreases as the hidden layer grows (`r b("item", "width")`), or for the class effect, which barely changes (`r b("class", "width")`). In the linear condition width is spent on the item effect at the class effect's expense (`r b("item", "width", "linear")` against `r b("class", "width", "linear")`); the interaction grows with width there too (`r b("interaction", "width", "linear")`) but stays small throughout.

Where no interaction is planted, a ReLU learner still represents one: the measured value is small (median `r addint(max(toy$d))` at the widest layer) but its interval excludes zero in `r addflag(max(toy$d))` of runs, against a nominal 5%. The linear arm cannot do this at any width, since a linear map of additive inputs is additive.

The amount of overlap is also affected by the width of the hidden layer as well: For the ReLU models, the wider the hidden layer, the less the item and class effects share directions (`r b("item_class", "width", kindv = "overlap")`). Similarly, the overlap between the interaction and the item-class subspace follows the same pattern (`r b("int_margins", "width", kindv = "overlap")`). The linear models show a different pattern, however. The item-class overlap shows no effect as a function of width, and the interaction effect's overlap with the item-class space grows as a function of the width (`r b("int_margins", "width", armv = "linear", kindv = "overlap")`), climbing from `r fv("int_margins", 8, "linear", "overlap")` to `r fv("int_margins", 256, "linear", "overlap")` times chance. It approaches chance without reaching it, and both overlaps stay below chance at every width under the linear learner (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-capacity}). Smaller hidden layers thus do not merely represent less of the interaction, they also force the components onto shared directions.

# Experiment 2: Language Models {#sec-exp2}

Experiment 1 asks what a learner represents when we control the composition of its language; Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate} separately demonstrates that the measure recovers structure planted directly in a representation. Neither speaks to how a transformer represents real language, which is the question Experiment 2 asks. Experiment 2 applies the same decomposition to the contextual representations of pretrained language models, across two linguistic categories: part of speech and grammatical role.

## Dataset {#sec-exp2-data}

In order to examine the separability of linguistic representations in models, we examined two linguistic categories: part of speech and grammatical role. For both, we concatenate six general-domain English Universal Dependencies treebanks [@nivre2020ud], giving `r cm(gsf("ud_corpus", "n_sentences", 41095))` sentences and `r cm(gsf("ud_corpus", "n_pre_grid_tokens", 706323))` word tokens; Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-stimuli} provides the full breakdown. We measure two model families at three matched scales: OPT-BabyLM, trained on developmentally plausible quantities of child-available language [@warstadt2023babylm; @houghton2026holisticstorageverb+up], and Pythia, trained on the Pile [@biderman2023pythia], at 125M/160M, 350M/410M, and 1.3B/1.4B parameters, with widths of 768, 1024, and 2048. Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-models} gives parameter counts and training-token estimates.

## Stimuli {#sec-exp2-stimuli}

Our stimuli comprise two linguistic categories: part of speech ([noun]{.smallcaps} versus [verb]{.smallcaps}) and grammatical role (*nsubj* versus *obj*, restricted to nouns). For each category we select items that occur in both of its classes, such as *walk*, which occurs as both a noun and a verb. An item is a single inflected word form, not a lemma, so different inflections of one lemma are separate items: *walk* and *walking* are both items, each included only if it is itself attested in both classes. Pooling them under one lemma would collect *walk* and *walks* into a single item, and the two classes would then be comparing different tokens, which the embedding layer could then separate before any contextualization has occurred. Capitalization is ignored when occurrences are grouped, but not in the text the models read, so a sentence-initial *Walk* counts toward the item *walk* and is tokenized as it appears there.[^5]

[^5]: OPT-BabyLM's tokenizer is uncased, so this choice has no effect for that family of models. On the other hand, Pythia's tokenizer is not uncased; however, lowercasing the input would be the larger distortion, since a sentence-initial word is capitalized in written English which the model was trained on.

An item is included only if it occurs at least ten times in each class. This yields `r max(llm$n_items[llm$construction == "POS (noun/verb)"])` items for part of speech and `r max(llm$n_items[llm$construction == "role (subject/object)"])` for grammatical role, with median counts per class running from `r stimrange()` (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-stimuli}), inside the range we validated for the measurement (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate}).

## Method {#sec-exp2-method}

The decomposition, the two reported quantities, and the replication logic are identical to Experiment 1. For every token we extract the hidden state of the word's last subword at every layer of each model.[^6]

[^6]: Almost every item is a single subword, so this choice has little bearing on the results: zero items are split into multiple subword tokens under Pythia's tokenizer, and only eight are split under OPT-BabyLM's tokenizer.

Transformer hidden states contain a few rogue dimensions whose means and variance are both disproportionately high [@timkey2021bark], and these would otherwise dominate any subspace estimated from the raw embeddings, so we divide each dimension by its standard deviation before decomposing (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-standardize}).

## Results {#sec-exp2-results}

The results for the final layer are reported in Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-llm}; the layer-by-layer results are shown in @fig-llm.

The item effect is the largest component in both categories, running from `r ldrng("POS (noun/verb)", "size_item", 3)` for part of speech and `r ldrng("role (subject/object)", "size_item", 3)` for grammatical role. Similarly, the effect of class is mostly comparable across the two linguistic constructions (`r ldrng("role (subject/object)", "size_class", 3)` vs `r ldrng("POS (noun/verb)", "size_class", 3)` for part of speech and grammatical role respectively). On the other hand, while the interaction effect is larger than the class effect for part of speech (`r ldrng("POS (noun/verb)", "size_int", 3)`), the same is not true for grammatical role (`r ldrng("role (subject/object)", "size_int", 3)`). This may indicate that part of speech is more lexicalized than grammatical role, perhaps unsurprisingly.

Another way to describe these results is with respect to the whole representation rather than the item-by-class structure: the item effect accounts for `r gr("ga")` of what varies in a token, the class effect `r gr("gb")`, and the interaction `r gr("gg")`, with the remaining `r gr("gctx")` being specific to the context a word appears in (See Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-llm}).

Both the class effect and the interaction effect increase as a function of layer depth. The interaction is essentially absent at layer 0 in both categories, between `r allrange("size_int", deep = FALSE)` across every category and model, and rises to between `r allrange("size_int")` (@fig-llm). This is not surprising since at the first layer, the model has yet to integrate enough context to commit to the class of the representation. The increase in the effect across layer depth is also not an artifact of the learned absolute position embeddings: zeroing OPT-BabyLM's leaves the class structure more word-specific rather than less, and Pythia, which encodes position with rotary embeddings inside attention rather than an additive input embedding, shows the interaction at least as strongly (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-positions}).

Turning to how those components are oriented, the class direction carries almost none of the item effect. At the deepest layer, item-class overlap runs `r ldrng("POS (noun/verb)", "leak")` for part of speech and `r ldrng("role (subject/object)", "leak")` for grammatical role, so projecting out the class direction leaves more than 99% of the item effect intact. While both overlaps are technically less orthogonal than a random subspace, the overlap itself is tiny, so the two are near-orthogonal rather than exactly orthogonal.

In contrast to the main effects, the interaction effect is not orthogonal to class or item. Across the six models, `r ldrng("POS (noun/verb)", "leak_int", 3)` of the interaction for part of speech is in the span of the two main effects, and for grammatical role `r ldrng("role (subject/object)", "leak_int", 3)` is, against nulls whose upper ends run `r ldrng("POS (noun/verb)", "leak_int_null", 3)` and `r ldrng("role (subject/object)", "leak_int_null", 3)` respectively. The smallest of these overlaps exceeds the largest of the nulls, so the pattern holds in every model. In other words, the small departure from orthogonality between item and class becomes a large one for the interaction.

In the artificial learner the components become meaningfully orthogonal once the hidden layer is wide enough for the structure, but LLMs don't follow that same pattern: their components remain meaningfully non-orthogonal at every scale (`r ovr("leak")` times chance for the item effect into the class direction and `r ovr("leak_int")` for the interaction into the margins), and increasingly so as width grows. Added width there is spent representing more of the language rather than giving the same structure more room.

```{r}
#| label: fig-llm
#| fig-width: 3.05
#| fig-height: 2.65
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Fraction of the representation (ignoring context) accounted for by each component, summing to 1, against relative depth from the embedding layer (0) to the final layer (1). Each line is one model; color is the training corpus, linetype the hidden width, shading the 95% interval."
# Built by hand rather than pivoted, because each component carries its own re-split interval.
band <- function(d, val, lo, hi, label) {
  tibble(construction = d$construction, family = d$family, scale = d$scale, depth = d$depth,
         component = label, share = d[[val]],
         lo = if (is.null(lo)) NA_real_ else d[[lo]],
         hi = if (is.null(hi)) NA_real_ else d[[hi]])
}
plt <- llm
plt <- bind_rows(
  band(plt, "size_item", "size_item_lo", "size_item_hi", "item"),
  band(plt, "size_class", "size_class_lo", "size_class_hi", "class"),
  band(plt, "size_int", "size_int_lo", "size_int_hi", "interaction")) |>
  # Short labels, matching @fig-toy. Spelled out they are longer than the row is tall, and the
  # rotated strip text clipped mid-word ("class effec").
  mutate(component = factor(component, c("item", "class", "interaction")))
# Color separates the two corpora, linetype the three matched widths, so each of the six lines
# is identifiable rather than three of them sharing one color. The shaded band is each model's
# re-split 95% interval; it is narrow enough to read as a thickening of the line, which is the
# point: the spread that matters here is between models, not within a measurement.
ggplot(plt, aes(depth, share, color = family, linetype = scale,
                group = interaction(family, scale))) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = family), color = NA, alpha = .3,
              show.legend = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .55, alpha = .85) +
  facet_grid(component ~ construction, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(BabyLM = UO[["gold"]], Pythia = UO[["blue"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(BabyLM = UO[["gold"]], Pythia = UO[["blue"]]), guide = "none") +
  # Labelled by the hidden width the pair shares rather than by the two parameter counts:
  # four characters instead of nine, and it is what the caption says the linetype encodes.
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("125M/160M" = "dotted", "350M/410M" = "dashed",
                                   "1.3B/1.4B" = "solid"),
                        labels = c("768", "1024", "2048"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, .5, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 3) +
  labs(x = "relative depth", y = NULL) +
  # With the short width labels both legends fit on one row, so they sit side by side rather
  # than stacked. The rotated row labels drop a point to keep clear of the panel beside them.
  theme_paper(7) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside", legend.box = "horizontal",
        legend.spacing.x = unit(4, "pt"), legend.key.width = unit(11, "pt"),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(size = 7))
```

# Experiment 3: Probing the Interaction {#sec-exp3}

Experiment 2 shows that lexical representations contain an idiosyncratic component that can't be separated out into simple item and class representations, but neither shows what information is contained within the interaction. An item-by-class term captures any reliable difference between a word's uses in the two classes, and some of that difference may be correlated with the context, since subjects appear in different constructions from objects.

## Method {#sec-exp3-method}

We test whether the interaction encodes class information by probing its representation. If $\gamma$ encodes the class, the class should be recoverable from the part of a token's representation that is neither the item effect nor the shared class direction, and we remove both explicitly. All probing happens *within* a single word, so we ask whether *walk*'s noun uses can be told from *walk*'s verb uses; the item effect is constant within a word and so cannot contribute. We then estimate $\beta$ as the difference between the two class means pooled over all items, normalize it, and remove that component from every token, so that whatever separates the classes afterwards is not the direction they share.

What remains after removing those components is the interaction: the part of a word of a specific class that is neither a fact about the word nor a fact about the class. We fit a cross-validated logistic probe to it, five folds, with classes balanced by subsampling within each word so that chance is 0.50, and average the resulting accuracies over words. We include tokens only if they have at least ten occurrences in each class, the same threshold the stimuli are selected on. The whole procedure is then repeated with the class labels permutated within each word, which preserves every word's token count and class balance while destroying the labeling so that we have an appropriate control [@hewitt2019control]. We run this at the deepest layer of the largest model in each family, for both categories.

## Results {#sec-exp3-results}

```{r}
#| label: dec-setup
#| include: false
dec <- bind_rows(
  rd("llm_decode_pos_form.csv") |> mutate(construction = "POS (noun/verb)"),
  rd("llm_decode_interaction.csv") |>
```
