```{r}
    filter(construction == "role") |>
    mutate(construction = recode(construction,
                                 role = "role (subject/object)"))) |>
  left_join(MODELS, by = "model") |>
  mutate(construction = factor(construction, c("POS (noun/verb)", "role (subject/object)")))
```

Results are reported in @tbl-decode. For all models, the class is recoverable from the interaction at well above chance, reaching `r g(dec$class_peritem[dec$construction == "POS (noun/verb)" & dec$family == "Pythia"], 2)` for part of speech and `r g(dec$class_peritem[dec$construction == "role (subject/object)" & dec$family == "Pythia"], 2)` for grammatical role, while the permutated null sits on chance. The null landing on chance is what makes those accuracies interpretable, since it is the same probe, the same folds, and the same word-level averaging with only the labeling destroyed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-decode
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy of recovering the class from the interaction, at the deepest layer of the largest model in each family, compared to the null; brackets are bootstrapped intervals."
dec |>
  arrange(construction, family) |>
  transmute(class = shortname(construction), model = paste(family, size),
            accuracy = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", class_peritem,
                            class_peritem_lo, class_peritem_hi),
            null = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", class_peritem_null,
                           class_peritem_null_lo, class_peritem_null_hi)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llll", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7)
```

The results demonstrate that $\gamma$ carries class information rather than generic correlated context.

# Discussion and Conclusion {#sec-discussion}

The present study examined whether a word's representation in a language model is exemplar-like or abstract and found that it contains elements of both. We decomposed a word's representation in a class into an item effect, a class effect, and a word-class interaction. The first two capture information shared across classes or words, respectively, while the interaction captures information specific to a particular word-class combination. In a model trained on an artificial language, we found an interaction effect even where the language itself was additive, so some of this structure comes from the architecture rather than from the language. Additionally, across six pretrained language models and two linguistic categories, we found a similar interaction effect in every model and category. The abstract components were nearly orthogonal, whereas the interaction overlapped with both, indicating that abstract and item-specific information are represented together rather than on separate axes.

Overall, the present results indicate that language model representations encode both abstract and item-specific structure, supporting generalization across words and classes while retaining information about specific combinations.

# Limitations {.unnumbered}

Our evaluation is restricted to English and relies on two linguistic categories tested across two model families (OPT-BabyLM and Pythia) at three parameter scales. While these choices cover a range of architectures and linguistic phenomena, broader typological, categorical, and architectural validation remains a direction for future work.

# The Artificial-Language Grid {#sec-appendix-grid}

Table \ref{tbl-grid} describes the language and the MLP parameters.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-grid
#| tbl-cap: "The Experiment 1 language parameters. The first five rows define each artificial language, the next two the learner MLP model. Item and class ranks are held fixed so that the interaction's rank is the only one that varies. Crossing every level gives 38,400 cells; the three languages in which all three effect weights are zero contain no item-by-class structure at all and are excluded, leaving the reported total."
.k <- toy$key |> strsplit("_") |> do.call(what = rbind) |>
  as.data.frame() |> lapply(\(x) sort(unique(as.numeric(x))))
lv <- function(x) paste(formatC(x, format = "g"), collapse = ", ")
tibble::tribble(
  ~factor,              ~levels,
  "item weight",        lv(.k[[1]]),
  "class weight",       lv(.k[[2]]),
  "interaction weight", lv(.k[[3]]),
  "context weight",     lv(.k[[4]]),
  "interaction rank",   lv(sort(unique(toy$r_int))),
  "hidden width",       lv(sort(unique(toy$d))),
  "activation",         "linear, ReLU",
  "seed",               lv(sort(unique(toy$seed)))) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "ll", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("factor", "levels")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8) |>
  pack_rows("language", 1, 5) |>
  pack_rows("learner", 6, 7) |>
  pack_rows("replication", 8, 8)
```

Item rank is fixed at `r unique(toy$r_item)` and class rank at `r unique(toy$r_class)`, so the structure a language requires is `r unique(toy$r_item) + unique(toy$r_class)` directions plus the interaction's rank, running from `r min(toy$rank)` to `r max(toy$rank)`. Of the `r cm(nrow(toy))` runs, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(toy$converged))` trained to convergence.


Every learner is trained in full batch with the Adam optimizer at a learning rate of 0.01, minimizing cross-entropy against the exact ground-truth distribution until the loss plateaus, on one GPU with twelve worker processes.

Both the size and the overlap models use weakly informative priors rather than the package defaults: a normal distribution with mean zero and standard deviation 2.5 on every population-level coefficient, a normal distribution with mean zero and standard deviation 1 on the standard deviations of the random effects, and an LKJ(2) prior on their correlation. The coefficient prior still covers the largest effects either model estimates, which reach about 2.8 on the logit scale, and the prior on the standard deviations is much wider than any variance component the data support, so neither prejudges a result.

@fig-toy-fit reports how well that training succeeded, and what it did not buy. The left panel is the Kullback-Leibler divergence from the learner's predictions to the ground-truth distribution, which is the cross-entropy at convergence minus the entropy of the target; the entropy floor itself varies across the grid, so the raw cross-entropy is not comparable between languages but this difference is. The right panel is the share of the item-by-class structure that the hidden layer actually carries, as a fraction of the share planted in the language. Both are restricted to the languages in which the interaction is more than 30% of the planted structure, which are the languages where the question has teeth.

```{r}
#| label: fig-toy-fit
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Fit and recovery against hidden width, for languages whose planted structure is more than 30% interaction. Left: Kullback-Leibler divergence from the learner to the ground-truth distribution, so zero is a perfect fit. Right: the interaction share measured in the hidden layer as a fraction of the share planted in the language, so one would be full recovery and the plotted values are the fraction of it reached. Lines are medians over runs with interquartile bands, which show how much the languages in the grid differ from one another rather than measurement error."
#|
ARMC <- c(ReLU = UO[["gold"]], linear = UO[["green2"]])

.fit <- toy |>
  filter(converged) |>
  mutate(planted_int = ach_int / (ach_item + ach_class + ach_int)) |>
  filter(planted_int > 0.30) |>
  mutate(recovered = size_interaction / planted_int,
         wpos = as.integer(factor(d, sort(unique(d)))))

bind_rows(
  transmute(.fit, act, wpos, panel = "divergence from the language (0 = perfect fit)", y = fit_gap),
  transmute(.fit, act, wpos, panel = "interaction recovered (1 = all of it)",         y = recovered)) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, c("divergence from the language (0 = perfect fit)",
                                 "interaction recovered (1 = all of it)"))) |>
  group_by(act, panel, wpos) |>
  summarize(med = median(y), lo = quantile(y, .25), hi = quantile(y, .75), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(wpos, med, color = act, fill = act)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = .16, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .7) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = ARMC, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ARMC, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_along(sort(unique(toy$d))),
                     labels = sort(unique(toy$d))) +
  labs(x = "hidden width", y = NULL) +
  theme_paper(9) + theme(legend.position = "top",
                         legend.margin = margin(0, 0, -6, 0),
                         panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# The Decomposition {#sec-appendix-math}

![Each word in each class is observed in many contexts, and those observations are averaged to give that word's representation in that class. Every one of these averages is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and every item appears in every class.](fig-grid.pdf){#fig-grid width="100%"}

A word used in a given class is observed in many contexts, and the representation differs a little in each. Averaging those observations gives that word's representation in that class: for items $i \in \{1,\dots,I\}$ crossed with classes $c \in \{1,\dots,C\}$, $M[i,c] \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the mean representation of item $i$ in class $c$ (@fig-grid). The three components are read off that grid (@fig-replication).

![The three components across the grid of words and classes. An item effect is one value per word, the same in every class; a class effect is one value per class, the same for every word; and the interaction differs for every word in every class.](fig-replication.pdf){#fig-replication width="100%"}

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Validating the Measure {#sec-appendix-validate}

Experiment 1 defines a ground truth language, however, it cannot distinguish a failure of the measure from the model representing the language differently than the structure it was given. Here we remove that ambiguity by constructing representations in which $\mu$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are set directly, with no model or training, and passing the result through the same analysis used for the language models. Ground truth therefore exists at the level where the measure operates.

```{r}
#| label: setup-validate
#| include: false
val <- rd("validate_measure.csv")
v_rec <- val |> filter(n_obs == 24, d >= 768) |> group_by(planted_int) |>
  summarize(n = n(), measured = median(size_interaction),
            lo = quantile(size_interaction, .025), hi = quantile(size_interaction, .975),
            flagged = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop")
v_null <- bind_rows(
  val |> filter(planted_int == 0) |> group_by(n_obs) |>
    summarize(effect = "interaction", med = median(size_interaction),
              p95 = quantile(size_interaction, .95),
              flagged = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_class == 0) |> group_by(n_obs) |>
    summarize(effect = "class effect", med = median(size_class),
              p95 = quantile(size_class, .95),
              flagged = mean(size_class_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_item == 0) |> group_by(n_obs) |>
    summarize(effect = "item effect", med = median(size_item),
              p95 = quantile(size_item, .95),
              flagged = mean(size_item_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"))
# False-positive rate of the re-split test BY WIDTH: how often a truly-zero effect's interval
# excludes zero. This is what says whether a small measured effect at a given width is a real
# detection or the test's own floor, and it tells the reader where the test is calibrated.
v_fp_d <- bind_rows(
  val |> filter(planted_int == 0, n_obs == 24) |> group_by(d) |>
    summarize(effect = "interaction", fp = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_class == 0, n_obs == 24) |> group_by(d) |>
    summarize(effect = "class", fp = mean(size_class_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_item == 0, n_obs == 24) |> group_by(d) |>
    summarize(effect = "item", fp = mean(size_item_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"))
fpget <- function(eff, dd) v_fp_d$fp[v_fp_d$effect == eff & v_fp_d$d == dd]
v_ov <- val |> filter(!is.na(leak_item_into_class), n_obs == 24, planted_overlap == 0) |>
  group_by(d) |> summarize(measured = median(leak_item_into_class),
                           lo = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .025),
                           hi = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .975),
                           chance = median(k_class / d), .groups = "drop")
# The power side: a KNOWN fraction of the class direction placed inside the item subspace. The
# measured overlap should rise above chance and be flagged outside its own random-orientation null.
v_ov_power <- val |> filter(!is.na(leak_item_into_class), n_obs == 24, planted_overlap > 0) |>
  group_by(d) |> summarize(measured = median(leak_item_into_class),
                           lo = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .025),
                           hi = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .975),
                           chance = median(k_class / d),
                           detected = mean(leak_item_into_class_outside %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE")),
                           .groups = "drop")
vget <- function(eff, obs, col) v_null[[col]][v_null$effect == eff & v_null$n_obs == obs]
```

Specifically, we generated representations with known values of $\mu$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$, varying the number of items, classes, representation dimensions, observations per word and class, and noise level across the range used in the experiments. Components were centered to satisfy their defining constraints and rescaled to predetermined shares of the total squared length. The grid included the same factorial Experiment 1 run: the three components measured in Experiment 2, item counts from 27 to 180, two and four classes, widths from 8 to 2048, 10, 24, and 100 observations per item and class, three noise levels, and five seeds. We also generated orthogonal and known non-orthogonal item and class effects: the orthogonal condition draws $\alpha$ and $\beta$ independently, while the non-orthogonal condition places a known fraction of $\beta$ along $\alpha$'s largest dimension. In total, this gave `r cm(nrow(val))` runs.

At 24 observations per item and class, the measured interaction matches the one it was given across the whole range (Table \ref{tbl-val-recovery}), and is flagged in essentially every run where anything was present and about one in twenty where nothing was.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-recovery
#| tbl-cap: "Recovery of the interaction at 24 observations per item and class in 768 or more dimensions, pooled over noise levels, item counts, and widths. *Specified* is the interaction share built into the generated representations and *measured* the median share recovered, with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across runs in brackets; *flagged* is the share of runs whose re-split interval excludes zero."
v_rec |>
  transmute(`specified` = g(planted_int, 3),
            runs = n,
            `measured` = sprintf("%.4f [%.4f, %.4f]", measured, lo, hi),
            `flagged` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * flagged)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

All three effects read essentially zero when a component is set to zero, at every sample size, and each is flagged at approximately the nominal 5% rate (Table \ref{tbl-val-null}).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-null
#| tbl-cap: "What the measure reports when an effect is set to exactly zero, by observations per item and class, pooled over every other axis of the validation grid. *Median* and *95th pct* summarize the measured share of that effect across runs, and *flagged* is the share of runs whose re-split interval excludes zero, which should sit near the nominal 5%."
v_null |>
  transmute(effect, observations = n_obs,
            median = g(med, 5), `95th pct` = g(p95, 4),
            flagged = ifelse(is.na(flagged), "---", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * flagged))) |>
  arrange(effect, observations) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

The false-positive rate varies somewhat with representation width and component, particularly at small widths, but remains below 10% throughout the validation grid except for the class effect at the narrowest width, where it reaches 14% (Table \ref{tbl-val-fpd}). The language-model analyses use $d\geq768$, where the rates are closer to the nominal level.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-fpd
#| tbl-cap: "How often a component set to exactly zero is flagged, by width and by effect."
v_fp_d |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = effect, values_from = fp) |>
  transmute(`width d` = d,
            item = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * item),
            class = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * class),
            interaction = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * interaction)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-overlap
#| tbl-cap: "Item-class overlap when the two effects are constructed orthogonal, at 24 observations per item and class. *Measured* is the median overlap across the runs at that width with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles in brackets; *chance* is the overlap expected if the component were randomly oriented, $r/d$ for a target subspace of $r$ dimensions in a representation of width $d$."
v_ov |>
  transmute(`width d` = d, measured = ci(measured, lo, hi, 5),
            `analytic chance` = g(chance, 5)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

With orthogonal item and class effects, the measured overlap tracks the chance level across representation widths (Table \ref{tbl-val-overlap}). When a known fraction of the class direction is placed inside the item subspace, the measured overlap rises above chance and is detected in `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * v_ov_power$detected[v_ov_power$d == 2048])` of runs at $d=2048$ (Table \ref{tbl-val-power}). Thus, the measure recovers both the expected chance overlap under orthogonality and genuine non-orthogonality.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-power
#| tbl-cap: "Measured item-class overlap when a fraction of the class direction is placed inside the item subspace (non-orthogonal), at 24 observations per item and class. *Measured* is the median overlap across the runs at that width with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles in brackets; *chance* is the overlap expected if the component were randomly oriented, $r/d$ for a target subspace of $r$ dimensions in a representation of width $d$; *detected* is the fraction of runs whose overlap falls outside that null's 95% interval."
v_ov_power |>
  transmute(`width d` = d, measured = ci(measured, lo, hi, 4), chance = g(chance, 5),
            detected = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * detected)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

## Variance across contexts {#sec-appendix-spread}

The interaction is a residual, and a residual absorbs whatever noise the terms before it do not. A word's average representation in one class is taken over the contexts it appears in there, so it contains some amount of sampling error; estimated within a single split, the interaction would inherit that error and grow with the variance across contexts whether or not any interaction was present.

The cross-split dot product eliminates this bias. The two estimates come from disjoint halves of a word's tokens in that class, so their errors are independent and mean-zero, and the expectation of their inner product is the true squared length with no variance term: the context variance enters the variance of the estimate and not its expectation. This holds for any variance, and for a variance that differs from one word and class to the next.

Table \ref{tbl-val-noise} demonstrates this. Holding the planted interaction fixed and raising the variance across contexts to fifty times the variance between words and classes leaves the measured value where it is, and where nothing was planted the false-positive rate stays at the nominal level rather than rising with that variance. If anything the measure drifts slightly low at the largest variance.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-noise
#| tbl-cap: "Recovery of the interaction across simulations with different amounts of noise, in 768 or more dimensions, pooled over item counts, widths and sample sizes. *Specified* is the interaction share built into the representations and *noise* the variance across contexts per observation as a multiple of the variance between words and classes, so at 1x the two are equal. *Measured* is the median interaction share recovered across runs and *flagged* the share whose re-split interval excludes zero, which should sit at 5% in the rows where nothing was planted."
val |> filter(d >= 768, planted_int %in% c(0, 0.1, 0.2)) |>
  group_by(planted_int, noise_ratio) |>
  summarize(runs = n(), measured = median(size_interaction),
            flagged = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop") |>
  transmute(specified = g(planted_int, 2), noise = paste0(g(noise_ratio, 0), "x"),
            runs, measured = g(measured, 4),
            flagged = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * flagged)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrrr", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("specified", "noise", "runs", "measured", "flagged")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

# Width and Orthogonality {#sec-appendix-capacity}

Whether the item and class effects are orthogonal depends on the width of the representation. @fig-toy-overlap reports that relationship from the fitted models; this appendix gives the remaining properties of the artificial-language runs.

Under ReLU, overlap stays below chance at wide layers and rises above it as the layer narrows, while the linear condition stays well below chance at every width.

The two summaries that follow are descriptive medians across runs rather than estimates from the fitted models. At low widths, the representations vary substantially across runs, with this variability decreasing as width increases. For example, two runs of the same language differ by `r g(seedspan(8, "item"), 2)` in the item effect and `r g(seedspan(8, "class"), 2)` in the class effect at width 8, compared with `r g(seedspan(32, "item"), 2)` and `r g(seedspan(32, "class"), 2)` at width 32. This variability reflects the different ways models can distribute information when representational capacity is limited.

Two properties of the language also affect the composition of the item-by-class structure (Table \ref{tbl-lang}). Increasing the effect of context reduces the interaction share, while increasing the item's share in the language produces a corresponding increase in its share of the representation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lang
#| tbl-cap: "How two other properties of the artificial language move the composition of the item-by-class structure, under ReLU, pooled over widths. Rows within a property partition the same runs. Values are medians of the three shares over the runs in the row."
toy_bylang |>
  transmute(property, level, runs,
            item = g(item, 3), class = g(class, 3), interaction = g(interaction, 3)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

# Stimulus Counts {#sec-appendix-stimuli}

The six general-domain English Universal Dependencies treebanks [@nivre2020ud] we concatenate are EWT [@silveira2014ewt], GUM [@zeldes2017gum], LinES [@ahrenberg2007lines], ParTUT [@sanguinetti2015partut], GENTLE [@aoyama2023gentle], and PUD [@zeman2017pud].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-constructions
#| tbl-cap: "Stimuli for the two linguistic categories, with the two classes of each in parentheses. *Item types* is how many word forms occur in both of them at least ten times; forms occurring in only one are excluded. *Median tokens* is how often a typical form occurs in each of its two classes, in the order they are listed."
tibble::tribble(
  ~class,                                  ~`item types`,
  "part of speech (noun / verb)",          max(llm$n_items[llm$construction == "POS (noun/verb)"]),
  "grammatical role (subject / object)",   max(llm$n_items[llm$construction == "role (subject/object)"])) |>
  mutate(`median tokens` = c(stimmed("pos_noun_verb_form"),
                             stimmed("role_nsubj_obj"))) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrl", linesep = "", escape = FALSE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Model Details {#sec-appendix-models}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| tbl-cap: "The six models, paired by width. Training-token counts are approximate; the OPT-BabyLM models train for 20 epochs over a 100M-word corpus, which is roughly 150M tokens, so their effective token exposure is about twenty times that."
tibble::tribble(
  ~family,  ~model,          ~params, ~width, ~layers, ~`training data`,     ~`tokens`,
  "BabyLM", "opt-babylm-125m", "125M",   768,      12, "BabyLM (child-available)", "~3B",
  "BabyLM", "opt-babylm-350m", "350M",  1024,      24, "BabyLM (child-available)", "~3B",
  "BabyLM", "opt-babylm-1.3B", "1.3B",  2048,      24, "BabyLM (child-available)", "~3B",
  "Pythia", "pythia-160m",     "160M",   768,      12, "the Pile",                 "~300B",
  "Pythia", "pythia-410m",     "410M",  1024,      24, "the Pile",                 "~300B",
  "Pythia", "pythia-1.4b",     "1.4B",  2048,      24, "the Pile",                 "~300B") |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrlr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1, latex_hline = "major")
```

The six models are listed in @tbl-models. The two families are matched on width rather than on parameter count, which is what the measure is sensitive to: the chance level for overlap is the class subspace rank over the width, so a comparison across models of different width has to be read against different chance levels. Pairing at 768, 1024, and 2048 removes that from the family comparison.

They differ in two ways that matter elsewhere in the paper. The training corpora differ by more than two orders of magnitude in size, which is the manipulation of interest. They also use different mechanisms for representing the position of each token: Pythia uses rotary embeddings, applied inside attention, while OPT learns absolute position embeddings added at the input. Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-positions} uses that difference to rule out absolute position as the source of the interaction.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Standardizing the Hidden States {#sec-appendix-standardize}

Rogue dimensions could in principle affect what we measure. Table \ref{tbl-standardize} reports part of speech at the deepest layer, measured both with and without the per-dimension rescaling.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-standardize
#| tbl-cap: "Part of speech at the deepest layer, measured with and without the per-dimension rescaling. Sizes are shares of the item-by-class structure; overlaps are the raw fractions, not multiples of chance."
rd("llm_unified_form.csv") |> filter(init == "pretrained") |>
  group_by(model) |> filter(layer == max(layer)) |> ungroup() |>
  left_join(MODELS, by = "model") |> arrange(family, scale) |>
  transmute(model = paste(family, size),
            si = g(std_size_interaction, 3), ri = g(raw_size_interaction, 3),
            sc = g(std_size_class, 3), rc = g(raw_size_class, 3),
            so = g(std_leak_item_into_class, 4), ro = g(raw_leak_item_into_class, 4)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrrr", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("model", "std", "raw", "std", "raw", "std", "raw")) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "interaction" = 2, "class effect" = 2,
                     "item-class overlap" = 2)) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Deepest-Layer Measurements {#sec-appendix-llm}

Table \ref{tbl-llm} gives the results of the overlap measurement at the final layer along with the null.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-llm
#| tbl-cap: "Overlap measurement and the null values at the final layer of each model. Each overlap is the fraction of one component lying inside another's subspace: the item effect inside the class subspace, the interaction inside the span of the two main effects. Each is followed by the overlap divided by its own null, so 4.2x means the overlap is 4.2 times what random orientation gives."
llm |> group_by(construction, model) |>
  filter(layer == max(layer)) |> ungroup() |>
  arrange(construction, family, scale) |>
  # One row per model. A median across the six hid exactly what the six are being compared for,
  # and the sizes' re-split intervals are far narrower than the spread across models, so pooling
  # them reported a precision that belonged to a single measurement rather than to the set.
  # Each overlap is against its own model's null rather than r/d: the two differ, since r/d
  # assumes the subspace has its algebraic maximum rank while the projection uses the rank
  # actually fitted, roughly half of it for the marginal subspace.
  transmute(class = shortname(construction),
            model = paste(family, size),
            o1 = ov1(leak, leak_null_med, 4),
            n1 = g(leak_null_med, 4),
            o2 = ov1(leak_int, leak_int_null_med, 3),
            n2 = g(leak_int_null_med, 3)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrr", linesep = "",
      col.names = c("class", "model", "item-class overlap", "its null",
                    "interaction overlap", "its null")) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 7) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

Table \ref{tbl-output} reports each component's share at the final hidden layer alongside the same measurement after the unembedding, on the same tokens. A hidden layer is only meaningful relative to what reads it, and a linear map whose gain differs across directions does not preserve shares, so the two need not agree. The interaction's share is close to stable in both categories, moving by at most 0.045, so the claims we make about it do not depend on where it was measured. The main effects shift somewhat for part of speech, where the class effect takes a larger share of the structure after the unembedding than it holds in the hidden layer.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-output
#| tbl-cap: "Each component's share of the item-by-class structure at the final hidden layer and after the unembedding, measured on identical tokens. Both members of a pair are point estimates from one run, which is what makes them comparable to each other; they therefore sit about 0.003 from the re-split medians quoted elsewhere."
# Built from the hidden and output rows joined side by side, rather than pivoted, so that each
# component's pair sits together and the table reads as six comparisons rather than twelve rows.
local({
  w <- function(k) outl |> filter(where == k) |>
    select(model, construction, item = size_item, cls = size_class, int = size_interaction)
  inner_join(w("hidden"), w("output"), by = c("model", "construction"),
             suffix = c("_h", "_o")) |>
    left_join(MODELS, by = "model") |>
    arrange(construction, family, scale) |>
    transmute(class = shortname(construction), model = paste(family, size),
              i_h = g(item_h, 3), i_o = g(item_o, 3),
              c_h = g(cls_h, 3),  c_o = g(cls_o, 3),
              n_h = g(int_h, 3),  n_o = g(int_o, 3)) |>
    kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrrrr", linesep = "",
        col.names = c("class", "model", rep(c("hidden", "output"), 3))) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7) |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "item effect" = 2, "class effect" = 2,
                       "interaction" = 2)) |>
    collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
})
```

## How much of a token the components account for {#sec-appendix-gain}

The fraction of squared length reported for each measurement demonstrates how much a representation comprises item, class, or interaction components relative to each other. However, it does not say how much of the entire representation comprises that information. In this section, we calculate how much of the overall representation each component takes up (Table \ref{tbl-gain}). We operationalize this by estimating how much of a token's hidden state each one accounts for as the reduction in squared error against guessing the grand mean. The components are orthogonal, so their contributions accumulate, and the three do not sum to the whole, since most of what varies in a token is the context it appears in.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gain
#| tbl-cap: "How much of a token's hidden state each component accounts for, at the deepest layer, as the percentage reduction in squared error against guessing the grand mean."
llm_gain |>
  arrange(construction, family, scale) |>
  transmute(class = shortname(construction), model = paste(family, size),
            word = g(100 * ga, 1), cls = g(100 * gb, 1),
            int = g(100 * gg, 1)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrr", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("class", "model", "word", "class effect", "interaction")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Positional Embeddings Are Not the Source {#sec-appendix-positions}

In theory, one possible architectural explanation for the interaction could be the way in which position is represented within the models. Specifically, the BabyLMs add a *learned absolute position embedding*. The two classes of a linguistic category are not positionally interchangeable in a sentence, since subjects precede objects and nouns and verbs typically occupy different slots, so a representation that varies with position varies with the class. If that is what the decomposition is picking up, the interaction would be an artifact of the position rather than their representation.

In order to rule this out, we re-extracted every OPT-BabyLM model with the positional embeddings zeroed out. Pythia encodes position with rotary embeddings applied inside attention rather than an additive input embedding, so this analysis was run only for the BabyLMs.

We rule out the effect of position by comparing the class effect to the interaction for the models with positions intact and positions zeroed out. We operationalize this as the class effect divided by the sum of the class effect and the interaction, which we call the *portable fraction*. The three shares sum to one by construction, and zeroing the embeddings drives the item share up sharply, which pushes the class effect and the interaction down together for reasons unrelated to the split between them. Dividing one by their sum holds the item share out of the comparison. If positions were manufacturing the interaction, removing them should mitigate or eliminate the interaction effect and increase the effect of class, so the portable fraction should rise.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-posabl
#| tbl-cap: "Trained OPT-BabyLM at the deepest layer, with absolute position embeddings intact and zeroed. Sizes are shares of the item-by-class structure and the portable fraction is the class effect divided by the sum of the class effect and the interaction."
# Read from the main POS file. It carries the *_noposemb inits for every OPT-BabyLM
# size under the current estimator, so this table is on the same footing as every
# other table in the paper. (An older, separate ablation CSV used to hold these rows
# but was written by a superseded measure.py; it has been removed.)
rd("llm_unified_form.csv") |>
  filter(grepl("babylm", model), grepl("^pretrained", init)) |>
  group_by(model, init) |>
  slice_max(layer, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(model = sub(".*/", "", sub("-20eps-seed964", "", model)),
            positions = ifelse(grepl("noposemb$", init), "zeroed", "intact"),
            class = std_size_class, interaction = std_size_interaction,
            portable = std_size_class / (std_size_class + std_size_interaction)) |>
  arrange(match(model, c("opt-babylm-125m", "opt-babylm-350m", "opt-babylm-1.3B")),
          desc(positions)) |>
  transmute(model, positions, `class` = g(class, 3), `interaction` = g(interaction, 3),
            `portable fraction` = g(portable, 3)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

Removing the position embeddings makes these representations *less* separable, not more. The portable fraction falls in every model, from `r pf("125m", "intact")` to `r pf("125m", "zeroed")`, from `r pf("350m", "intact")` to `r pf("350m", "zeroed")`, and from `r pf("1.3B", "intact")` to `r pf("1.3B", "zeroed")` (Table \ref{tbl-posabl}). Whatever the absolute position embedding contributes, it is contributing to the part of class structure that *is* carried by a shared direction. Take it away and what remains is more word-specific, not less. The interaction is not an artifact of position.
